title: The man born blind (John 9:1–12)
hook: mud on the eyes, wash in Siloe, and he comes back seeing

segments.voice: Yesterday, ego eimi, the wrong tense on purpose: before Abraham was made, I am. Your line was I am.

When something terrible happens, the question comes fast: whose fault is it? A child is born sick, and a relative wonders aloud what the parents did. It's an old reflex, and the disciples have it too. Walking along, they pass a man who has been blind since birth, begging by the road. And they ask Jesus, as if the man weren't there: Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind? Jesus refuses the question, and then he bends down to the dirt.
screen: `WHOSE FAULT IS IT?` → `A MAN BLIND FROM BIRTH.` → `WHO SINNED, HIM OR HIS PARENTS?`

segments.voice: His answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents; but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Neither. He won't hand out blame. He doesn't explain why the man was born blind; the text never does. He turns the question from why did this happen to what will God do here. Then he says again what he said at the feast: as long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. And he does something earthy. He spits on the ground, makes mud, and spreads it on the man's eyes. Some early Christian writers saw an echo of Genesis, where God shapes the first man from the dust: the one who made eyes in the beginning is making them again. Then: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloe, which is interpreted, Sent. He went therefore, and washed, and he came seeing." He isn't healed on the spot. He has to walk, blind, mud on his face, to the pool. Siloe, Siloam in other Bibles, means sent, and just before this Jesus has spoken of him that sent me. The pool's name points back at the one doing the healing. The early Church heard baptism in this story. Justin Martyr called baptism illumination, and the Church still reads this Gospel in Lent with adults preparing to be baptized at Easter.
screen: `NEITHER HE NOR HIS PARENTS.` · `MUD FROM THE DUST, ON HIS EYES.` · `SILOE: WHICH MEANS SENT.` · `BAPTISM AS ILLUMINATION.` · then, large: `HE WENT, AND WASHED, AND CAME SEEING.`

segments.voice: If you can, go to a sink, or just cup your hands and imagine water in them, and bring it slowly to your face, over your eyes, holding your hands there a moment. Then open your eyes and look at what's in front of you as if for the first time. If you pray, ask to see clearly; if not, notice what washing feels like when you pay attention.
Siloe. The pool whose name means sent, where the man born blind went to wash after Jesus put mud on his eyes. Today's word.
Your line: go, wash. Not whose fault, but what God will do here. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the man born blind on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in Year A, used with the scrutinies for adults preparing for baptism at Easter.

chat.says: In that story, was the man born blind because he or his parents sinned?
options: Jesus says neither; he won't hand out blame, and turns to what God will do there.
His parents had, Jesus says, but he forgives them and heals their son anyway.
The man had, Jesus says, and washing in the pool was the penance for it.
chat.meaning: Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents. Jesus won't hand out blame; he turns from why it happened to what God will do.

Siloe.meaning: the Douay's name for the pool whose name means sent

Siloam.meaning: the same pool's name in other Bibles

Justin Martyr.meaning: an early Christian writer who called baptism illumination

Lent.meaning: the season of preparation before Easter

notes: Genesis 2:7 echo in the mud: found in Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.15) among others; stated as 'some early Christian writers'. Confirm.
Pool of Siloam: discovered in 2004 during sewer repair work; identified as the Second Temple pool. Confirm.
Baptism as 'illumination' (phōtismos): Justin Martyr, First Apology 61. Confirm.
Fourth Sunday of Lent, Year A, with the second scrutiny. Confirm.
